In the primitive state where we imagine the sun it resembled the nebulae that the telescope shows us composed of a nucleus more or less brilliant surrounded by a nebula which, condensing at the surface, ought to transform it some day into a star. If one conceives by analogy all the stars formed in this manner, one can imagine their anterior state of nebulosity itself pre- ceded by other stars in which the nebulous matter was more and more diffuse, the nucleus being less and less luminous and dense. Going back, then, as far as possible, one would arrive at a nebulosity so diffuse that one would be able scarcely to suspect its exist- ence. Such is indeed the first sta

phere; sometimes the nebulous matter, by condensing in a uniform manner, has produced the nebulae which are called planetary. Finally a greater degree of condensation transforms all these nebulae into stars. The nebulae classed accord- ing to this philosophic view indicate with an extreme probability their future transformation into stars and the anterior state of nebulosity of existing stars.
